video_title: Jim Al-Khalili on Time, Quantum, Biology, and Cosmology | Mindscape 366
gist: Physicist Jim Al-Khalili argues the mainstream picture of time is upside down: because no real system is ever truly isolated, irreversibility and the arrow of time are fundamental, and the time-symmetric equations (Schrödinger, Newton, Maxwell) are idealized special cases of open-system master equations. He extends this into a proposed quantum replacement for the past hypothesis — the universe began in a very low entanglement-entropy state — and into quantum biology, where his group models proton quantum tunneling in DNA hydrogen bonds as a mutation mechanism, while arguing physics undergraduate teaching should be rebuilt around entanglement, decoherence and open systems rather than square wells and harmonic oscillators.

insights.claim: Jim Al-Khalili holds that time is a real, tangible constituent of four-dimensional spacetime rather than merely 'the thing clocks measure,' and that its direction is baked into the universe rather than being a human perceptual artifact.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Sets the frame for his whole research program: if directionality is fundamental, the standard emergence-from-time-symmetric-laws story is the thing that needs explaining away, not the reverse.
insights.quote: for me time is a real thing. It's tangible.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili distinguishes 'physical time' (the parameter entering the equations of physics) from 'manifest' or psychological time (the perceived flow), and treats reconciling the two as an unsolved problem he has no answer to.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A clean partition that lets physicists claim progress on the arrow of time while conceding zero progress on the felt passage of time — useful for judging overclaims in popular physics.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili accepts an arrow of time but denies that physics contains any 'flow' of time, saying the flow does not exist even though we perceive it.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Separates two claims routinely conflated in public discussion: directionality (defensible in physics) versus flow (a perceptual claim with no equation behind it).
insights.quote: An arrow may exist, but the flow of time doesn't exist. And yet we perceive it to flow.

insights.claim: Trained in relativity, Al-Khalili leans eternalist — all times exist the way all points of space do — but declines to hold a strong position on presentism versus eternalism.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Shows how physics training biases metaphysical priors: the block-universe intuition follows from years of doing relativity, not from an independent argument.
insights.quote: So, eternalism I guess is what I'd naturally feel is the the right way of thinking about things.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili argues that even if time turns out to be emergent from something deeper such as quantum entanglement, that would not make it unreal — unlike temperature, which he says disappears when you zoom in on the molecules.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Draws a line between 'emergent' and 'illusory' that most quantum-gravity popularizations blur; a useful test to apply to claims that 'time does not exist.'
insights.quote: I think if time is emergent, then nevertheless, it's a a real tangible thing.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili claims time would still be passing in a heat-death universe trillions of years hence, even with nothing left to measure it — a position close to Newtonian absolute time, modulo relativity of reference frames.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A sharp test case separating operationalist views of time (no clock, no time) from substantivalist ones; he plants himself firmly on the substantivalist side.
insights.quote: So even if nothing is changing, time is still passing. It's just that you don't you can't measure.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili inverts the standard explanatory order: rather than deriving irreversibility from time-symmetric fundamental laws, he treats irreversibility as the more fundamental fact and time-symmetric laws as idealizations.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: This is the episode's core contrarian bet; he concedes it is a minority position among physicists, which makes it a marker for tracking a possible shift in foundations research.
insights.quote: is that it's the other way around, that time's direction, directionality, irreversibility is more fundamental.

insights.claim: The load-bearing argument for irreversibility-first is that time-symmetric dynamical equations apply only to isolated systems, and no system in the universe is truly isolated except the universe as a whole.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: The whole thesis rests on this one premise — attack or defend it and the rest follows; it also explains why he sees decoherence and cooling as the same kind of fact.
insights.quote: because nothing is truly isolated in our universe, there's there's an inevitable directionality arrow of time

insights.claim: Al-Khalili explicitly proposes no change to any known equation — not Schrödinger's, Einstein's, Maxwell's or Newton's — only a change of default context from closed to open systems.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Distinguishes this from crank physics: it is a reframing of which formalism is 'basic,' making it empirically conservative but pedagogically radical.

insights.claim: In this framing the Schrödinger equation is a special case of the open-system master equation, because an isolated system is a special case of an open system — reversing the usual textbook hierarchy where open-system dynamics are derived as add-ons.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable restatement of the thesis in formal terms — and the hook for his argument about how quantum mechanics should be taught.
insights.quote: an isolated system is a special case of an open system

insights.claim: Carroll pushes back that any open system can be embedded in a larger isolated one from which the open-system equations are derived, but grants that promoting the open-system view to front and center is a legitimate change of perspective.
insights.speaker: Sean Carroll
insights.so_what: Identifies the strongest standard objection: the inversion may be a change of emphasis rather than of physical content.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili concedes that a system in thermal equilibrium with its environment has no perceptible arrow of time, and rescues his view by insisting that any such system-plus-environment is itself nested inside a still larger environment.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Exposes the regress in the argument: the arrow is always borrowed from one level up, which is exactly why the universe-scale case still needs a past hypothesis.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili concedes that for the entire universe there may be no arrow of time and that time symmetry may hold, which forces him to accept that the universe still began in a special state.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: The irreversibility-first program does not eliminate the need for special initial conditions — a limitation he states openly rather than papering over.
insights.quote: I I agree that for the entire universe, there may there is no arrow of time or there is time symmetry, which is why I still think we have an issue

insights.claim: Even idealized isolated systems only lack an arrow of time once they reach equilibrium; an isolated system prepared far from equilibrium still exhibits entropy increase.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Clarifies that isolation alone does not buy time-symmetry — the initial condition does the work, which is the same lever the past hypothesis pulls.

insights.claim: The past hypothesis works by pushing the required 'special moment' of low entropy all the way back to the Big Bang so there is no earlier time for the symmetric equations to run backwards into, but the cost is breaking time translation invariance by designating one moment as special.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: States the price of the standard solution explicitly — it trades one asymmetry for another rather than deriving the arrow from nothing.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili argues the past hypothesis should not be counted as an extra assumption but folded into the existing fine-tuning problem, alongside the values of the speed of light, the constants of nature and the strengths of the forces.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A cost-accounting move: if low initial entropy is just one more initial condition, it stops being a uniquely embarrassing postulate.
insights.quote: I I would argue that the past hypothesis simply part of that. It's not an It's not an additional uh uh sort of requirement or assumption on top of the initial conditions

insights.claim: Cosmologists resolve the puzzle of a hot dense early universe already in thermal equilibrium by noting gravity was left out: gravitational entropy was extremely low in a smooth expanding universe.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: The standard answer to the most common objection to low-entropy beginnings; necessary background for his own addition below.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili proposes 'fusion entropy' as a distinct and underappreciated middle step in the entropy story: the universe expanded and cooled too fast to fuse beyond hydrogen and helium, leaving an enormous reservoir of unrealized low entropy locked in the strong nuclear force and waiting for stars to form.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A specific, nuclear-physics-flavored contribution to the entropy narrative that runs alongside gravity — and a concrete reason the universe is still far from equilibrium.
insights.quote: there's still that very very low fusion entropy locked into I guess the the the the nature of the strong nuclear force. It's there waiting to happen.

insights.claim: Without fusion entropy, the Sun would have clumped, died and reached maximum entropy long ago; nuclear fusion is the reason the Sun remains a usable low-entropy source today.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Ties the availability of free energy for life directly to nuclear physics rather than to gravity alone.
insights.quote: The fact that it's still a source of low entropy is because of nuclear fusion.

insights.claim: Carroll argues life is not a struggle against the second law but a mechanism that exploits it, using free energy from the Sun to maintain structure, organization and metabolism far from equilibrium; Al-Khalili agrees.
insights.speaker: Sean Carroll
insights.so_what: Corrects a widespread popular-science inversion; the operative resource is low-entropy photons in, high-entropy photons out, not resistance to entropy.
insights.quote: No, that's exactly backwards. Life is taking advantage of the second law of thermodynamics.

insights.claim: Carroll is skeptical of the claim that life exists to help the universe increase entropy, noting entropy will increase anyway and there is no law requiring it to increase as fast as possible; Al-Khalili adds that if life is confined to Earth, the universe would be relying on one tiny planet to do that job.
insights.speaker: Sean Carroll
insights.so_what: Undercuts maximum-entropy-production framings of life that circulate in complexity science and origin-of-life work.
insights.quote: There's there's no law that says it increases as fast as possible.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili identifies as a realist and explicitly not a Copenhagenist, despite being trained by two staunch Copenhagen-school PhD supervisors in the 1980s.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A generational marker: foundations questions were career-risky in the late 1980s and are now mainstream, indicating how fast the norms in this field have moved.
insights.quote: is that I'm not a Copenhagenist. That I'm a realist.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili insists the interpretations of quantum mechanics cannot all be right and that one is objectively correct — rejecting the pragmatic pluralism of picking an interpretation by convenience — while declining to say which one it is.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A clear methodological stance: interpretations are factual claims about nature, not lenses to be swapped, which raises the stakes on experimental discrimination between them.
insights.quote: they can't all be right, you know. Either there are uh parallel worlds or there aren't.

insights.claim: Although not a supporter of Everettian many-worlds, Al-Khalili concedes it is the simplest and cleanest resolution of the measurement problem because decoherence alone does the work of separating outcomes.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A skeptic conceding the opponent's main virtue is a stronger signal about many-worlds' standing than an advocate's endorsement.
insights.quote: I'm I'm not the biggest supporter of Everettian many worlds quantum mechanics, but I do have to admit it is the simplest cleanest way of describing the measurement problem.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili decomposes measurement into three stages — choice of basis, entanglement with the environment producing decoherence, and the appearance of a single outcome — and argues only the third stage requires an interpretation.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A clean triage that localizes the genuinely contested part of the measurement problem, and makes clear no observer with a PhD is required — any environment measures.

insights.claim: Decoherence does not make Schrödinger's cat alive or dead; it removes the interference between the branches, leaving both a live and a dead cat, which is precisely why a third interpretive step is still needed.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: The single most commonly muddled point in popular quantum accounts — decoherence solves the interference problem, not the outcome problem.
insights.quote: Decoherence doesn't cause the cat to be either dead or alive. What it does is get gets rid of the the the mixture. It gets rid of the the um the interference between them.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili treats consciousness-causes-collapse as a discarded position the field has moved past.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A field-consensus signal worth citing against the persistent commercial and popular use of quantum-consciousness framings.
insights.quote: But the idea of you know, consciousness causing collapse of the state and things like that, I think we've sort of grown beyond that now.

insights.claim: Both agree entanglement per se is reversible — entangling with a single qubit can be undone — and that irreversibility arises only when a system entangles with enough degrees of freedom that reversal becomes impractical, making the quantum arrow of time a statistical-mechanical effect.
insights.speaker: Sean Carroll
insights.so_what: Directly relevant to quantum error correction and computing: reversibility is a resource that degrades with environmental coupling, not a binary property.
insights.quote: Once you entangle with enough things, you effectively in practice lose the ability to reverse it.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili rates the quantum decoherence/entanglement arrow of time as the most irreversible and non-negotiable of the several arrows of time, ranking it above the thermodynamic and causal arrows.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: This ranking is what motivates his attempt to build a quantum past hypothesis rather than a thermodynamic one.
insights.quote: The The The The quantum uh entanglement or quantum decoherence arrow of time, which we talked about, for me is the best, the most irreversible, non-negotiable one-way process

insights.claim: Al-Khalili notes he never needed to commit to a quantum interpretation to do productive research, either as a nuclear reaction theorist or in quantum biology, while still treating the wave function as something real that evolves in time.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Illustrates that interpretation-independence is workable for calculation while realism about the wave function still matters for how one models energy transport in cells.

themes.theme: Quantum Biology and DNA Proton Tunneling

insights.claim: Al-Khalili defines quantum biology narrowly as non-trivial quantum mechanics — long-lived coherence and entanglement — explicitly excluding the trivial sense in which all chemistry is quantum, and frames the research question as whether life evolved to exploit or to suppress quantum effects.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A definitional filter that separates legitimate quantum biology claims from marketing; apply it to any 'quantum' biotech claim.
insights.quote: Quantum biology is the non-trivial quantum mechanics, you know, long-lived quantum coherence and quantum entanglement

insights.claim: The field started for Al-Khalili in the late 1990s when molecular biologist John Joe McFadden proposed that adaptive mutations in E. coli — where bacteria preferentially mutate in the direction the environment favors — might be explained by a quantum superposition collapsed preferentially by measurement; most of the physics department thought it was crazy.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Documents the origin and initial reception of a now-hot field — a template for how fringe interdisciplinary claims become fundable research programs.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili's group at Surrey has focused for several years on quantum tunneling of the proton in the hydrogen bonds holding DNA's two strands together: the proton normally sits more stably on one side of an energy barrier, and if it tunnels across before the strands unzip during replication, that can produce a mutation.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A concrete, falsifiable quantum-biology mechanism with direct implications for mutation-rate modeling — distinct from the vaguer coherence claims in the field.

insights.claim: The DNA proton-transfer idea traces to Swedish physical chemist Per-Olov Löwdin, who published in the early 1960s that the proton in a DNA hydrogen bond might cross via quantum tunneling rather than thermally over the barrier.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Establishes a 60-year provenance for the mechanism, countering the impression that quantum biology is a recent fashion.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili reports that the calculations have grown steadily more sophisticated as computational chemists add ingredients to large simulations, and that the story keeps changing — he says he has been left behind by his own collaborators' codes.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A candid signal that the quantitative result on DNA tunneling is not settled — treat any headline claim about its magnitude as provisional.
insights.quote: and the story keeps changing

insights.claim: Al-Khalili's answer to the standard 'warm and wet' objection — that biological systems at 300 K decohere in femtoseconds — is that life may have evolved to fine-tune its environment so it is non-Markovian, with information flowing back from the environment to sustain the quantum state rather than draining it.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Non-Markovianity is a measurable property; this converts a hand-waving objection into a testable engineering claim potentially relevant to room-temperature quantum devices.
insights.quote: technically we say the environment isn't Markovian. There's some non-Markovianity. So, the environment is itself it it's helping keep the quantumness going

insights.claim: Al-Khalili ties the biology back to the arrow of time: if life engineers its environment to sustain coherence, it is effectively deferring the onset of a directionality of time for that quantum subsystem for as long as possible.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: The novel synthesis of the episode — coherence lifetime reframed as local resistance to the arrow of time, linking foundations to biology.

insights.claim: Carroll frames the quantum-computing analogy: engineers spend large sums to maintain entanglement among a few qubits and have only been trying for a few years, whereas nature has had billions of years to find working strategies; Al-Khalili endorses the analogy and credits it to thinkers like Seth Lloyd.
insights.speaker: Sean Carroll
insights.so_what: If biological systems maintain coherence at 300 K through environmental engineering, the mechanism is a potential template for room-temperature quantum hardware.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili grades the current evidence unevenly: quantum tunneling in enzymes moving particles around has been experimentally confirmed, whereas whether quantum mechanics plays a role in photosynthetic light absorption remains an open question.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A rare explicit confidence ranking within quantum biology from an insider — photosynthesis is the field's most-cited example and he does not treat it as settled.
insights.quote: That's all been experimentally confirmed. They they utilize things like quantum tunneling.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili calls magnetoreception the 'poster child' of quantum biology: the only theory in town for bird navigation posits a pair of entangled electrons in a molecule in the eye, one knocked onto a neighboring atom by an incoming photon, whose singlet/triplet spin populations are sensitive to the Earth's magnetic field.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Notable that it is the field's flagship case yet rests on being the only available theory — a monopoly of explanation, not a confirmation.
insights.quote: there's the poster child of quantum biology, which is the uh uh idea of magnetoreception

insights.claim: Al-Khalili stresses that entanglement is not a force: in the magnetoreception mechanism nothing tugs on the distant electron; what matters is how the external magnetic field shifts the relative populations of singlet versus triplet spin states.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: The standard popular framing of entanglement as spooky action is precisely what makes quantum-biology claims sound magical; both speakers concede they lack a good lay explanation.
insights.quote: Quantum mechanics isn't magic, right?

insights.claim: Al-Khalili and philosopher of physics Eddie Chen (UC San Diego) published a paper proposing that quantum entanglement and decoherence supply a more fundamental past hypothesis than the thermodynamic one: the universe began in a very pure quantum state rather than merely a very ordered one.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A specific, citable research proposal to watch — it would replace a coarse-graining-dependent postulate with a basis-independent quantum one.
insights.quote: what if the universe uh rather than just saying the universe started in a very ordered state, we say the universe started off in a very pure quantum state.

insights.claim: The chosen measure is entanglement entropy, motivated by the fact that a pure state has zero von Neumann entropy overall, yet its subsystems can acquire nonzero von Neumann entropies as they become entangled — the subtracted quantity being the entanglement entropy.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Names the concrete mathematical object doing the work, making the proposal checkable rather than rhetorical.

insights.claim: Under this proposal the fundamental cosmic story is not thermodynamic entropy increasing but everything becoming gradually more and more entangled with everything else from an initially low-entanglement-entropy state.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Reframes cosmic history as a monotonic growth of entanglement — a picture with direct overlap with holography and quantum-gravity research programs.
insights.quote: we we have tried to argue is that the universe started off with very low entanglement entropy

insights.claim: Al-Khalili flags the unresolved weak point of the entanglement-entropy proposal: entanglement entropy depends on how you divide the universe into subsystems, and there is no principled answer to how finely to carve it up.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: The factorization problem is the obvious attack surface; any serious follow-up work must solve it, so its absence is a useful progress marker.
insights.quote: the difficulty there is how how big are those subsystems? How how how much do you have to divide them up

insights.claim: Al-Khalili candidly rates the state of that program as unfinished and 'fluffy' — no follow-up paper has been published, with big gaps remaining, largely because both authors moved to other work.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: An honest status report: the idea is a stub, not an established alternative — relevant to anyone weighing how much traction the quantum past hypothesis actually has.
insights.quote: at the moment it's a bit fluffy and we haven't followed up that paper with anything else

insights.claim: Carroll notes a shared failure mode of theorists: publishing a suggestive paper and expecting others to extend it, then realizing nobody will and the follow-through is your own job.
insights.speaker: Sean Carroll
insights.so_what: A practical read on why promising foundations ideas stall — the bottleneck is author follow-through, not merit, which affects how to weight one-off speculative papers.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili argues the standard undergraduate quantum curriculum — one-dimensional Schrödinger equation, square wells and barriers, harmonic oscillators — must change, and that entanglement and decoherence should be taught because quantum technologies now depend on them.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A concrete curriculum gap between what physics graduates learn and what the quantum-technology industry needs — a hiring and training bottleneck worth tracking.
insights.quote: why the heck aren't we teaching students about entanglement and decoherence, you know?

insights.claim: Teaching entanglement and decoherence necessarily requires teaching open quantum systems, which Al-Khalili concedes may be too hard for a first course but should be standard by a later undergraduate course or graduate level.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Specifies where in the curriculum the change would have to land — a practical, actionable version of the abstract open-systems thesis.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili notes physicists are being forced to retrain by field: astronomers and cosmologists into advanced statistical analysis for large survey datasets, and others into computer science, AI and machine learning as those become the working tools.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A signal on where technical skill demand is shifting inside physical science — data-analysis and ML competence is becoming table stakes, not a specialization.
insights.quote: Other physicists are having to learn a lot of computer science and AI and machine learning, because that's the tool they're using.

insights.claim: Carroll argues that fixing interdisciplinary gaps — physicists not knowing philosophy of physics, or basic statistical model comparison — requires formal structures for cross-talk, not just exhortations to read more.
insights.speaker: Sean Carroll
insights.so_what: Points to institutional design rather than individual effort as the lever for interdisciplinary quality — relevant to how research programs and grants are structured.
insights.quote: I think we need to actually talk to each other. And and there should be more formal structures to allow that to happen.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili's interdisciplinary time research was funded by a large John Templeton Foundation grant, which he attributes to his public-engagement profile; he says Templeton funds speculative areas that ordinary public funding bodies are reluctant to touch, and that the grant required a substantial public-engagement component.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Maps the actual funding channel for foundations-of-physics work: private philanthropy plus a science-communication track record, not conventional grant agencies.
insights.quote: that is is uh not afraid to sort of fund some of these more speculative areas of research, which the usual sort of public funding bodies are reluctant to do.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili observes that philosophers of physics he collaborates with — Simon Saunders at Oxford, Eddie Chen at UC San Diego, Karim Thébault at Bristol — all hold PhDs in theoretical physics, which he sees as the grounding in mathematical physics needed to avoid fluffy work.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Quantifies a credentialing pattern: the productive physics-philosophy interface runs through people dual-trained in both, not through disciplinary outreach.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili took early retirement from Surrey at 63 in part because UK university budget pressure — Surrey was tens of millions in deficit and physics had to shed academic positions — and because the internal politics were becoming toxic.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: A first-hand data point on UK university financial distress forcing headcount cuts in physics, alongside separately acknowledged US funding difficulties.
insights.quote: And it became apparent that physics had to lose, actually lose academic positions

insights.claim: Al-Khalili notes theoretical physicists are relatively cheap to keep on, which is why stepping back from a salaried academic role did not end his research — though losing his permanent position means he can no longer write grant proposals or serve as a primary PhD supervisor.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Illustrates the specific institutional levers that stop emeritus researchers from continuing programs — grant eligibility and supervisory rights, not cost or capability.
insights.quote: Theoretical physicists are relatively cheap.

insights.claim: Al-Khalili says many theoretical physicists turn to foundational problems late in their careers precisely because they no longer have to publish or perish and can afford to work on big questions rather than nitty-gritty output.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: Explains a structural selection effect in foundations research: it is disproportionately done by people insulated from publication metrics, which shapes both its pace and its risk profile.
insights.quote: a lot of physicists, particularly theoretical physicists, start to worry about some of these foundational problems in physics because time is finite, right? Time is running out and and I I don't have to publish or perish anymore.

insights.claim: Both close on the view that the persistence of unanswered basic questions about time since Aristotle and Augustine is not a failure of science, and that public value from science comes from technology and applications while the fundamental itch is scratched alongside it.
insights.speaker: Jim Al-Khalili
insights.so_what: The standard defense of basic research under taxpayer scrutiny, stated by someone who has just lived through university budget cuts.
insights.quote: It's a bit like doing a jigsaw puzzle, you know, the the joy is in doing the jigsaw puzzle, not in finishing it.
